note_sections.t: Persistent uncertainty regarding prostate cancer screening warrants re-evaluation after an earlier negative biopsy and a steady PSA course.

A 63-year-old civil engineer initially entered evaluation years ago after a mildly elevated PSA triggered a systematic biopsy that returned entirely benign. He currently experiences moderate lower urinary tract symptoms, notably nocturia twice nightly and a slightly weak stream, yielding an IPSS score of 10. Medical background includes well-controlled hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, treated with amlodipine, lisinopril, metoprolol, and atorvastatin, plus occasional paracetamol PRN for osteoarthritis. He maintains a 36 pack-year smoking history and drinks roughly 26 units of alcohol weekly. Daily fitness routines include a 20-minute walk. Beyond urological matters, he recently finished six physiotherapy sessions for mechanical lower back pain, keeps up with regular dental check-ups, and manages mild visual impairment requiring large-print materials. He lives with his wife; their adult children visit weekly, and he continues active involvement in local engineering consultancy projects.

DRE — texture: smooth and symmetric; consistency: normal; asymmetry/nodules: absent. Vital signs reveal a blood pressure of 142/80 mmHg and a regular heart rate of 67 beats per minute. General inspection shows no peripheral oedema, while abdominal palpation confirms the absence of suprapubic tenderness or palpable masses.
